body.text: Tanya Sarawagi and Suryesh K. Namdeo, “The Double Helix of Danger: Securing Synthetic DNA in India,” ORF Occasional Paper No. 569, Observer Research Foundation, August 2026.

India has a large and rapidly growing bioeconomy that was valued at US$165.7 billion in 2024. It contributes approximately 4.25 percent of national gross domestic product (GDP) and is projected to reach US$300 billion by 2030.[1] This remarkable growth, driven by the expansion of biotechnology startups, gene-synthesis facilities, and life-science innovation hubs, positions India as a global biotech leader. It is further supported by the ambitious BioE3 (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, and Employment) policy that was launched in August 2024 to establish India as a bio-manufacturing powerhouse.[2] However, the rapid growth in biotechnology also increases exposure to concerning dual use research and biosecurity vulnerabilities.[3]

The potential development and deployment of biological weapons pose a threat to India’s bioeconomy, public health, and national security. Biological weapons are recognised as a class of weapons of mass destruction, with the ability to cause enormous death and destruction.[4] Deliberate biological attacks are relatively easy to engineer, difficult to detect, and can be disguised as natural outbreaks, making them potentially catastrophic. Such attacks go beyond endangering public health; they can fracture economies, destabilise governance systems, and erode public trust in institutions. History shows that even small-scale biological incidents can generate disproportionate psychological and political consequences; for instance, the Anthrax attack in 2001 had long-term impacts on the United States (US) biosecurity strategy.[5] The dual-use nature of biotechnology adds to this danger, as innovations designed for medicine, agriculture, or environmental benefit can be misappropriated for harmful ends.[6]

In the Indian context, agroterrorism, or the intentional targeting of crops or livestock to weaken economies and disrupt societies, is a potential threat.[7] Deliberately releasing a modified crop pathogen may trigger famine-like conditions and collapse markets.[8] In 2025, the Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested a Gujarat-based doctor who was reportedly plotting a bio-terror attack using ricin, a dangerous toxin extracted from castor beans.[9]

Over the past few decades, the threat landscape has expanded beyond traditional bioweapons to include synthetic pathogens, gene-edited toxins, and digitally designed viruses that can be produced through commercially available deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) synthesis technologies.[10] These developments have blurred the line between legitimate research and potential misuse, creating an urgent need for robust oversight and standardised synthetic DNA screening mechanisms across the biotechnology sector.[11]

Synthetic DNA is central to advancements in synthetic biology and the biotechnology industry. It impacts health, climate change, and food security[12],[13] Once limited to specialised laboratories, it has become widely accessible through on-demand gene synthesis services and the proliferation of low-cost, decentralised benchtop DNA synthesisers.[a],[14] Easy access to this modern technology can resolve a variety of research issues noncanonically; however, it will also lead to the rise of new dual use research concerns (DURC), where synthetic DNA can be used for malicious purposes.[15] Provider-level biosecurity measures currently rely on DNA synthesis companies to screen both ordered sequences and the legitimacy of customers before fulfilling synthesis requests. These companies flag and restrict potentially hazardous sequences. However, as synthesis capabilities move to decentralised laboratory settings through benchtop DNA synthesisers, this point of control can be bypassed, as DNA sequences can be generated locally without passing through commercial providers. In 2017, a study by Canadian researchers directed global attention towards the potential misuse of synthetic DNA, where scientists were able to synthesise a pox virus similar to smallpox using synthetic DNA.[16]

Current safeguards for commercial nucleic acid synthesis hinge on two complementary screening categories. Customer screening verifies the identity and legitimacy of and intended use by the ordering party, distinguishing the provider, customer, principal user, and end user as defined by the administration for strategic preparedness and response.[17] Guidance recommends collecting identification data, performing restricted‑party checks, and flagging evasive behaviour, although there’s no universal legal mandate, leaving providers to rely on voluntary protocols.[18] Sequence screening entails comparing ordered DNA constructs to the databases of known pathogens, toxins, and controlled genetic elements. These databases draw upon the regulated pathogen and toxin lists maintained by national governments to guide their respective biosafety and export-control regimes. The International Gene Synthesis Consortium (IGSC), a voluntary industry body, employs a self-created data set used by member companies, namely, the Regulated Pathogen Database (RPD) to identify ‘sequences of concern’[b] (SOCs) during order screening.[19] The RPD compiles entries from multiple national and international sources, including the US Select Agent List,[c] the Australia Group’s Common Control List,[d] and the European Union (EU) list of dual-use items.[e] When an ordered sequence shows similarity to sequences of a regulated pathogen or toxin in the RPD, it is automatically flagged for further human review and verification by the provider.[20],[21]

Several leading DNA synthesis companies around the world employ both customer and sequence screenings to mitigate biosecurity risks in DNA synthesis. The IGSC Harmonised Screening Protocol and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) 2010 Screening Framework Guidance are examples of voluntary provider screening guidance frameworks.[22],[23] The HHS also released a draft framework, Screening Framework Guidance for Providers and Users of Synthetic Nucleic Acids, in 2023, recommending more stringent screening requirements.[24] Existing frameworks, largely designed for centralised DNA synthesis companies, employ these two safeguards. However, these are insufficient for decentralised benchtop synthesisers.

The International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science (IBBIS) Common Mechanism for DNA Synthesis Screening integrates both customer and sequence checks, building on IGSC-harmonised protocols and extending screening to shorter sequences and broader SOC definitions. [25],[26] The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act 2026 represents a noteworthy move towards strengthening and formalising biosecurity governance in the US, which will help establish global norms for both commercially ordered and benchtop DNA synthesis.[27]

Benchtop DNA synthesisers now enable localised, automated gene production directly from digital sequence files.[28] Several advanced systems can assemble large DNA fragments within hours and require little external oversight.[29],[30] Due to their affordability and rapid availability, these decentralised systems broaden access and accelerate research but leave gaps in screening responsibility. The US-based Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI) warns that decentralised synthesis will lower the visibility and accountability in global synthetic DNA manufacturing to quite an extent.[31] India’s market mirrors this shift towards decentralised DNA synthesis growth.[32] Companies face occupational safety and liability risks if harmful sequences are synthesised or mishandled, while malicious actors could exploit device firmware[f] or stored sequence data for unauthorised use. Technical risks include firmware or data compromise, such as the so-called substitution attacks in which digital sequence files are altered during synthesis to yield pathogenic fragments that cannot be detected by screening.[33] DNA synthesisers are included in the Australia Group Export Control List and should be regulated for their potential dual use risk.[34] However, minimal effort has been directed so far towards regulating them, as existing oversight mechanisms primarily focus on pathogen lists and export licensing rather than device-level screening standards or firmware integrity requirements.

Customer screening becomes much more difficult in cross-border DNA orders, where providers have limited ability to verify end users, institutional legitimacy, or intended use across jurisdictions with differing regulatory standards. This gap often widens due to the involvement of third-party distributors, which creates opportunities for regulatory arbitrage, allowing actors to exploit the least restrictive markets to bypass safeguards. In this context, export control frameworks become critical, but their current focus on listed pathogens and material rather than digital sequence orders and synthesis services limits their effectiveness in addressing emerging biosecurity risks. Moreover, much of the global governance architecture still relies on voluntary industry norms, with limited binding obligations specific to decentralised benchtop synthesis platforms.

A key challenge lies in the self-regulation approach, where individuals or groups set and follow their own safety and ethical standards without formal external oversight. This approach is encouraged within the Do It Yourself (DIY) biology community.[g] While it can encourage grassroots innovation, it may not adequately distinguish between low-risk experimentation and activities that require more oversight. Therefore, achieving the right regulatory balance that supports innovation while addressing the risks of unregulated or potentially harmful activities by non-state actors remains a challenge.

Concerns over the misuse of synthetic DNA gained formal policy attention in 2010, when the US HHS released its Screening Framework Guidance.[35] This Guidance established the twin principles of customer screening and sequence screening for DNA synthesis providers prior to order fulfilment, emphasising identity verification and pathogen-sequence detection. Before this, till around 2008, agencies would get informal interagency alerts. In response to the Guidance, the industry formed the IGSC, which voluntarily adopted the Harmonized Screening Protocol to address compliance gaps.[36] A few European countries have incorporated—or propose to include—synthetic DNA oversight into their broader biosecurity strategies, embedding synthesis screening within life-science governance frameworks at the state level.[37] In 2025, the EU proposed a Biotech Act that will explicitly address the synthetic DNA governance concerns.[38]

Outside the North Atlantic sphere, a few countries are taking initial steps to screen potentially dangerous DNA synthesis orders. A prominent example is Nigeria, which has incorporated voluntary screening measures into its 2022 National Biosecurity Action Plan, balancing innovation with governance.[39] South Korea has also highlighted the importance of DNA synthesis screening and given specific recommendations in a strategic report.[40] In China, the Biosecurity Law and its export control regulations implicitly addresses to address DNA synthesis governance for biosafety and biosecurity.[41],[42] These efforts collectively reflect the growing recognition of the need for synthetic DNA sequence screening as the synthetic DNA market continues to expand.[43],[44]

To coordinate these dispersed initiatives, the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science (IBBIS) launched the Common Mechanism in 2024—a global baseline to harmonise screening practices and data-sharing protocols.[45] Complementary efforts by the Engineering Biology Research Consortium (EBRC) and the RAND Corporation in the US have supported implementation of the earlier US government’s efforts, offering recommendations based on strategic reports and propagating best practices to strengthen provider screening, inter-agency coordination, and conformity assessment mechanisms.[46],[47]

Apart from these policy recommendations, multiple technical tools now underpin sequence and/or customer screening practices, including SeqScreen, Aclid, FAST-NA, UltraSEQ, and SecureDNA.[h] Each has a different approach to identify the SOCs (see Table 1). Table 1 also reveals that all these screening tools are primarily based in the Global North. The Global South lacks indigenous tools to create SOCs based on pathogens included in their national control lists. This dependence on a limited number of tools developed in the US or Europe may create biosecurity vulnerabilities and can result in potential underrepresentation of region-specific threats.

Collectively, these efforts mark a transition from voluntary, fragmented oversight towards a more structured global biosecurity regime that seeks to balance innovation with responsibility before synthetic DNA production becomes fully decentralised.
For potential biothreats, such as gene orders corresponding to regulated pathogen fragments, countries have adopted three overlapping models of risk screening and mitigation.

The first is mandated provider-level screening, in which legal frameworks require DNA synthesis companies to verify customer legitimacy and screen sequences against controlled-pathogen databases before delivery. The US exemplifies this model through the HHS framework supported by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).[57] Some EU states, such as France, now extend similar mandates through their health and interior ministries.[58]

The second is an industry baseline or self-regulatory model, led by networks such as IGSC. This creates voluntary yet globally influential screening standards that align providers, research institutions, and oversight agencies.

The third emerging paradigm is device-level safeguard integration, in which benchtop synthesiser hardware and software carry built-in controls, including local sequence screening, user authentication, usage logging, and automated alerts. The EU and RAND Corporation’s proposals advocate these technological interventions to reduce the risk of misuse even when synthesis occurs outside regulated facilities.[59]

In practice, these models, as represented in Figure 1, often operate in combination: the US coordinates government oversight with industry compliance; the UK integrates its Home Office, Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL), and public health agencies through shared governance; and international consortia such as the IGSC seek to harmonise these paradigms into a single interoperable system of oversight.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into DNA design pipelines has lowered technical barriers to synthesis, enabling both legitimate and malicious applications.[60] The same AI tools that support genuine research can be misused with minimal effort. Algorithms can be repurposed to design or modify harmful biological sequences, sometimes without a clear understanding of their final effects. When AI-driven design tools are combined with benchtop DNA synthesisers, the gap between digital design and physical DNA narrows.[61], [62]

A 2023 Science article reveals how AI-driven biological design tools expose vulnerabilities that could enable the creation of pathogen-related or toxic sequences.[63] It discusses how easily AI bypasses the existing screening system, highlighting the widening gap between current safeguards and future dangers, and emphasising the urgent need to prioritise safeguarding AI-enabled biological risks. Current provider-level sequence screening against a static SOC database relies on sequence similarity and is constrained by high false positives, making it vulnerable to AI-enabled modifications that preserve their cellular function while evading detection. This showcases the need for functional screening approaches that assess biological activity rather than sequence identity alone.

Cyber-biosecurity vulnerabilities further increase this risk. DNA design software, firmware embedded in synthesis instruments, and cloud-based sequence repositories represent potential points of exploitation.[64] Compromise at any of these layers could result in unauthorised sequence manipulation or data theft. Substitution attacks, demonstrated in recent biosecurity research, illustrate how malware can alter design files during synthesis to insert pathogen fragments into otherwise harmless constructs.[65] This type of ‘digital-to-biological crossover attack’ would bypass standard screening, creating physical biohazards without visible indicators of tampering.

In a plausible scenario, a research laboratory ordering a routine plant gene could inadvertently synthesise a fragment coding for a toxin domain. This would not only threaten laboratory personnel but could also spread into environmental or clinical settings, triggering local public health emergencies and compromising national security.[66], [67] The convergence of AI design autonomy and cyber vulnerabilities in DNA synthesis workflows represents a critical dual use frontier that demands integrated oversight across bioengineering and information security domains.

According to the IBBIS Global DNA Synthesis Map, out of over 1,000 synthetic nucleic-acid-providing companies, barely 69 screen DNA orders.[68] Therefore, assured compliance is lacking across most of the companies within the existing US and UK screening frameworks. As India positions itself as an emerging biomanufacturing hub, risks historically framed within the Global North context should be re-conceptualised for Indian realities. Accordingly, context-specific rules, regulatory frameworks, and policy instruments must be developed to effectively address them. In India, most DNA providers operate without conducting sequence or customer screening. India’s synthetic DNA ecosystem, while still relatively small, is expanding rapidly. A handful of domestic producers have begun narrowing the technology gap, but much of the national demand continues to be met through imports supported by Indian distributors, mostly from the US and China. This could create geoeconomic risks, given the foundational importance of synthetic DNA in biotechnology. For example, a disruption in supply due to tariff or non-tariff barriers could quickly paralyse large parts of the bioeconomy.

Few Indian companies offer end-to-end commercial DNA synthesis services. Some academic facilities, such as the nucleic-acid and peptide-synthesis platform at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bombay, demonstrate research-level capability but remain largely internal and are not scaled for commercial orders.[69] Efforts are being made to introduce enzymatic benchtop printers into Indian laboratories, signalling an early movement toward decentralised production. Presently, multinational providers collectively dominate the local supply chain through their Indian subsidiaries or distributors.[70] Market studies estimate that India’s DNA synthesiser segment, valued at about US$5.8 million in 2022, could reach US$22 million by 2030, driven mostly by benchtop instruments.[71] Domestic players are slowly emerging in the DNA synthesis space, an indication that a foundational industry base is taking shape.[72]

Despite this growth, India faces multiple regulatory and administrative gaps in synthetic DNA biosecurity governance. Institutional Biosafety Committees (IBSCs) currently assess biosafety (not biosecurity) risks in research projects within individual institutions, but there is no nationwide protocol for sequence or customer screening in the commercial or importer supply chain. The India Biosafety Knowledge Portal lists risk-management regulations and procedures for laboratory work but does not extend these to screening DNA synthesis providers.[73] There is also no defined mechanism to report suspicious DNA orders to a competent authority.[74] Research laboratories follow internal usage and ethics protocols but lack strong biosecurity oversight.

Another critical gap in India is the absence of a national SOC database, unlike countries such as the US and the UK that have well-defined SOC frameworks and lists.[75], [76] India also lacks sophisticated analytical infrastructure, such as AI-assisted function-aware screening to detect newly engineered or composite sequences.[77] Global screening of SOCs is necessary to prevent unregulated export of high-risk DNA fragments. Even minor oversights in screening diligence can enable the transfer of virulence genes or host-range determinants, creating a realistic pathway for accidental spread or deliberate misuse. India’s heavy reliance on imported synthetic DNA exposes it to domestic biosecurity risks due to vulnerabilities in foreign provider controls. Strengthening its verification systems and aligning them with international SOC governance is essential. India’s export control through the Special Chemical, Organisms, Material, Equipment and Technology list (SCOMET) highlights potentially dangerous pathogens, toxins, and genetic material, but lacks a strong mechanism for more elaborate review of synthetic DNA.[78] It has released ethical guidelines for the application of AI for biomedical research but does not have any regulatory measures to ensure safe AI-based technical development for synthetic DNA design and production.[79]

Device regulation is another weak point. India imports benchtop DNA synthesisers included in the Australia Group Control list of dual-use biological equipment and related technology and software but lacks regulatory and certification mechanisms to address biosecurity concerns.[80] This leads to potentially sensitive technology without any biosecurity enforcement mechanism.[81] At the industry level, professional associations have yet to develop enforceable biosecurity or synthesis screening standards. This reluctance might stem from the fact that many private providers operate in regulatory ambiguity, guided more by cost and convenience than explicit national norms.[82] Further, several small startups and service labs depend on expensive imported reagents or equipment, reducing the incentives and resources to invest in systematic biosecurity screening. There is also fear of excessive regulation.

Most importantly, India lacks a dedicated national agency or board to oversee biosecurity.[83] Without a mandated interagency mechanism, critical information sharing often depends on personal networks rather than formal systems, leading to gaps in stakeholder communication, which thwarts effective prevention and mitigation of biothreats. Awareness and training remain limited. Most IBSC members and institutional safety officers are not equipped to evaluate DNA sequence orders, and biosecurity is still largely absent from university curricula. This has led to a generation of researchers who, although technically competent, are institutionally unprepared to recognise and manage emerging biosecurity risks. India is also a large importer of synthetic DNA where voluntary industrial screening is mostly conducted by foreign providers, which creates a risk of foreign non-state actors obtaining access to its data, thereby gaining leverage.

Together, these gaps expose a mismatch between India’s strength in biotechnology and its coordinated efforts to establish a standardised synthetic DNA screening regime across providers, importers, and devices. The challenge is not lack of intent but the need for a coherent policy architecture that will bind research, industry, and security into a unified framework.

India’s next step should be to shift from fragmented awareness to coordinated prevention. The objective is not to reinvent the global framework but to localise it with structures that align with India’s institutional realities while being connected to international norms.

The Department of Biotechnology, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the Indian Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR), the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change (MoEFCC), and other relevant agencies should develop and co-curate a multi-sectoral SoC database, reflecting India’s ‘One Health’ priorities. The creation of an interoperable structured database is urgent to ensure synergy among relevant government agencies and to reduce potential security threats. This database should help detect potential bioterrorism, agroterrorism, and gain-of-function research-related sequence order.[i] It should be based on the SCOMET list.[84] Aligning DNA synthesis oversight with India’s National One Health Mission will ensure convergence across public health, veterinary, and agricultural biosecurity systems and transform synthetic DNA screening from a niche laboratory concern into a core component of national biosecurity.[85]
Establish a National DNA Synthesis Screening Cell

A National DNA Synthesis Screening Cell should be created under the existing Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) Secretariat, linked with the existing export control framework through the SCOMET list under the Directorate General of Foreign Trade. A coordinated institutional model, either anchored within the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) or the Directorate General of Foreign Trade, with inputs from other agencies, may be explored to effectively operationalise this cell. It should be regularly updated, based on expert inputs, and integrated with the Indian Biosafety Knowledge Portal and linked to an open-source, freely available customised screening platform, based on expert recommendations.[86] This entity should:
• Provide centralised screening services for domestic synthesis companies.
• Host a national SOC database.
• Act as India’s focal point for synthetic DNA biosecurity, coordinating with the relevant security, health, and agriculture agencies as well as international organisations.

A two-step verification mechanism can help address biosecurity concerns linked to synthetic DNA production. The first step would involve halting the printing of potentially harmful DNA as soon as any SOC is detected in the user input and sending an alert to the manufacturer to conduct a preliminary investigation. If suspicious activity is detected, the second step should be for the manufacturer to notify law enforcement agencies, which could be followed by a review by an interministerial joint working group, based on the nature and severity of the threat.[87] Depending on the outcome, authorities can choose to allow continued use, impose restrictions, or initiate compliance audits and enforcement actions.
Incentivise Industry Self-Regulation

Industry self-regulation will only work with clear incentives. A voluntary code of conduct modelled on IGSC norms for customer verification, sequence screening, and escalation should be linked to tangible benefits, such as eligibility for government grants, procurement preferences, or expedited regulatory clearances. Other countries employ similar incentives: in the US, federal agencies often prefer IGSC-compliant providers, and in the EU, adherence to safety standards strengthens access to cross-border research funding, which has led to increased adoption of norms internationally. India can adopt similar measures by offering ‘biosecurity-compliant provider’ certification, giving firms a market advantage in domestic and export supply chains. This approach builds industry ownership while raising baseline safety standards.
Strengthen and Empower Institutional Mechanisms

Academic institutes should integrate biosafety, biosecurity, and dual use ethics into life science and biotechnology curricula, emphasising case-based learning, ethical reasoning, and simulation exercises. This will cultivate a generation of researchers for whom responsible science will be a foundational skill. Scientific academies should also issue guidelines or declarations for safe, secure, and responsible use of life sciences. Institutional Biosafety Committees (IBSCs) should receive updated mandates and technical training to review projects with potential gain-of-function research, particularly those involving external DNA orders or AI-assisted design tools. They should be able to report their findings to the responsible, competent authorities easily to ensure timely response.
Advance Biosecurity Diplomacy

India should use Track 2 and 1.5 diplomacy, as well as structured academic and industry dialogues with countries and economic blocs such as the US, the EU, and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to share screening methods, harmonise terminology, and build cross-border trust in DNA procurement systems. This can also help align expectations between regulators, industry, and research communities across jurisdictions. Engagement through platforms such as the Australia Group, QUAD and India–EU Trade and Technology Council could provide useful frameworks. Biosecurity could be part of the QUAD and the India–US TRUST engagements, although they are yet to institutionalise focused screening standards, regulatory alignments, and structured technical collaboration. The US Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Bill could be leveraged within the India-US TRUST initiative and QUAD to promote safe, secure, and resilient DNA synthesis supply chains through shared standards and joint risk assessments.[88] Dedicated biosecurity dialogues with trained science diplomats will keep the issue technically grounded and action oriented.

In December 2025, India hosted the ‘50 Years of BWC: Strengthening Biosecurity of the Global South’ event, which brought together diplomats, national contact points, and technical experts from over 80 countries from the Global South. It was a notable confidence-building measure that underlined the value of institutionalised biosecurity dialogues.[89] The recent India–Russia joint statement during the 23rd annual India-Russia Summit that included a dedicated reference to the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) should be followed by structured strategic dialogues to translate commitments into practical cooperation on emerging biological risks.[90]

At the regional level, India could initiate a DNA synthesis security network that enables early warning, information exchange, and standardised screening protocols across laboratories and suppliers. Existing models, such as the Strengthening Institutions for Biosafety and Biosecurity in Africa (SIMBA), an initiative of Africa’s Centre for Disease Control, which focuses on regional capacity-building, information sharing, and harmonisation of biosecurity practices, could provide a template.[91] Similarly, ASEAN’s Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) risk mitigation frameworks demonstrate how regional groupings can coordinate standards, training, and response mechanisms for chemical and biological threats.[92] Finally, insights could be drawn from the proposed EU Biotech Act, particularly its emphasis on supply-chain resilience, strategic biotechnology autonomy, coordinated risk assessment mechanisms, and alignment of biosecurity standards across member states, elements directly relevant to cross-border DNA synthesis screening and dual-use oversight.[93]

India is entering a crucial phase in its biotechnology trajectory. As its bioeconomy expands rapidly, driven by private sector investments in synthetic biology and biomanufacturing, the risks associated with inadequate synthetic DNA governance are set to grow in parallel. Synthetic DNA governance remains fragmented, voluntary, and technologically underequipped for an era shaped by decentralised benchtop synthesis, AI-assisted sequence design, and emerging cyber-biosecurity threats. This gap is not just theoretical; it exposes national health systems, agriculture, and high-value R&D networks to risks that could compromise economic stability and erode international confidence in India as a trusted bio-manufacturing hub.

Strengthening DNA synthesis oversight is, therefore, both an economic and a strategic imperative. India’s current dependence on imported synthetic DNA means that near-term biosecurity safeguards must operate across the importer–end-user chain, including institutional biosafety committees, research laboratories, and commercial users. A bottom-up screening pathway, backed by a national SOC database and a centralised DNA Synthesis Screening Cell, would distribute compliance costs without imposing prohibitive barriers on industry or innovation. Over time, as domestic manufacturing scales up, the screening responsibility must extend to provider- and device-level controls aligned with Australia Group guidance and emerging global norms.

If India succeeds in building an interoperable framework that integrates biosafety, biosecurity, AI governance, and One Health surveillance, it can position itself not just as a leading producer of synthetic DNA but as a rule-maker in the global biosecurity architecture. Creating a robust ecosystem for designing, developing, manufacturing, and commercialising genetic sequences is essential for India to achieve technological sovereignty and reduce its geoeconomic vulnerabilities. Anticipatory governance measures involving modified firmware in benchtop DNA synthesisers and the integration of biosecurity-by-design principles within existing systems are also crucial to ensure safe and secure growth of the bioeconomy. Failure to act risks the country’s technology base outgrowing its security systems, inviting vulnerabilities that are far more costly to manage once exploited. The moment to embed security into innovation is now, before decentralised DNA synthesis becomes the norm rather than the exception.
Suryesh K. Namdeo is Senior Research Analyst at the Indian Institute of Science, where he currently leads the Bio-Responsibility Initiative.

[a] A ‘DNA synthesiser’ is a compact instrument that rapidly prints custom DNA based on sequences provided, ready to be used for further experiments.

[b] Nucleic acid sequences that encode for the genes responsible for the pathogenicity or virulence or any toxin secretion that might become fatal to a large mass of people, if spread accidentally or deliberately. Their synthetic production is a concern not just for national but global biosecurity. Examples of the sequences included in SOCs are Anthrax Toxin Components, which are responsible for toxin components of the Bacillus anthracis, and whole genomes of highly pathogenic viruses like Ebola and Nipah virus.

[c] The US Select Agent List contains the biological agents and toxins that have been determined to potentially pose a severe threat to human and animal health, plant health, or animal and plant products. https://www.selectagents.gov/sat/list.htm.

[d] The Common Control List is a collection of enlisted human, animal, and plant pathogens, as well as dual-use materials, equipment, technology, and software that provide a framework for effective chemical and biological trade controls between the members of the Australia Group.

[e] The European Union list of dual-use items is setting up a community regime for the control of exports, transfer, brokering and transit of dual-use items and technology. OJ L 134/1 (May 29, 2009), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2009/428/oj. It harmonises EU countries’ controls on sensitive exports, including cooperation on licensing and information sharing, and ensures that dual-use goods cannot leave the EU without proper authorisation.
[f] ‘Firmware’ is the permanent software programmed into a read-only memory, where the data or file can be accessed but cannot be modified.
[g] ‘Do It Yourself (DIY) Biology’ is where biological experimentation is conducted outside traditional institutional settings

[h] Aclid, UltraSEQ, and secureDNA are platforms that automatically screen synthetic DNA/RNA orders and customer credentials. SeqScreen and FAST-NA are the software toolkits available for synthetic DNA screening. SeqScreen is open-source whereas FAST-NA has a subscription model.
